newsitem.title: UK: Ageing Euro population to save not spend,bank says.
newsitem.headline: Ageing Euro population to save not spend,bank says.

text.p: An ageing European population will save furiously in the first half of the next century, causing a long period of low consumer spending, Lloyds Bank said on Monday.

The dramatic swing in saving patterns will knock whole economies off course, costing jobs and cutting growth across the continent but keeping the lid on inflation, Patrick Foley, Lloyds' chief economic adviser, said.
Over the next 15 years, working Europeans will save large amounts of their earnings to compensate for shortcomings in their pensions.
"When it comes, the initial saving surge is likely to lead to a prolonged period of depressed consumer demand," Foley said.
"The result is likely to be slow growth, perhaps recession, with the biggest slowdowns occurring in Germany, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands," Foley said.
Unemployment rates are likely to be high, inflation will fall further and short- and long-term interest rates will be very low, he added.

Britain and France will be hit less badly. "The UK has a strong pensions position relative to European counterparts and the eventual ratio of working to retired people will not be as low as other countries," Foley said.

The problem is that in 10 years' time the 50-64 years old group will be the largest in Europe, putting pressure on a dwindling workforce to fund an expanding pension base. By 2035, those beyond retirement age will begin to dominate.
Much depends on how quickly governments react to the looming crisis as public finances come under enormous strain, Foley said.
But as the demographic dynamic shifts again, the situation will eventually unwind.
"As growing elderly populations start to draw on savings, overall saving rates will fall dramatically, to zero in some countries," Foley said.

"This longer term collapse in saving will strengthen consumer demand relative to potential output, especially given declining workforces." That could, eventually, herald the end of an era of low inflation. -- Mike Peacock, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7708
